items.title: AI Agents in Sandboxes
items.summary: Limiting agent blast radius while vibe coding and in applications Image created by Nano Banana (not bad!) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ⚙️ Security Automation (Pre-AI). The Code . ⚙️ AI Automation . The Code . 🔒 Related Stories: Cybersecurity | Penetration Tests 💻 Free Content on Jobs | ✉️ Sign up for the Email List ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ In my last post I wrote about how someone who is a complete newbie to AI and not that technical could start writing software…but also demonstrating how having software development expertise can help improve the results. Hank’s First AI Program One of the things I mentioned you should be wary of is letting an agent have complete network and file system access to all the things. In this post I’ll give a high level overview of how I’m solving the problem of unrestricted agents. After about two minutes of using Amazon Q (now Kiro) I was like NOPE. You’re not getting all that access. NO WAY. Why? Prompt injection, for one thing: Considering the Likelihood and Impact of AI Chatbot Prompt Injection and Minimizing the Risk And in general AI agents taking actions I don’t expect or didn’t mean to authorize. Agents are very “creative” at finding ways to fulfill your tasks and solve problems in ways that are not exactly ideal. A specific Linux user with limited permissions I started off by trying to figure out how I could use a specific Linux user to run Q which only had permission to work in a specific project directory and could only access certain files and take certain actions. That’s the solution in a nutshell…but… Software architecture problems The next problem I had trying to use Amazon Q was that it was changing code I didn’t want it to change. I would build a complex architecture and it would start rewriting parts of the architecture I didn’t want it touch when I asked or a change. No don’t change that change this . Test problems Similar to architecture problems when I tried to run tests and have Q automatically fix the problems, it would change the TEST instead of fixing the CODE with the problem! Creative and all but…not exactly what I had in mind. Prompt harder doesn’t work Prompting harder to try to tell Q to do this and not do that (well I think it’s Claude actually but you know what I mean) did not seem to solve the problem. Sometimes Q reads some parts of the prompt but not others. Context rules don’t work I tried creating context and rules to get Q to follow them across multiple projects. Nope. Sometimes I could get it to work but reiterating the rules or getting Q to print out the rules and check off each one as it goes. I’m still struggling with these things but regardless if I could get that to work, it was not concrete enough for my security needs. And when you weren’t looking… It’s easy to miss something while vibe coding (at least for me) because I want to go fast and I started using multiple agents at once. More on that later. And though I was trying to watch each action I had Q completely delete some of my code multiple times. This led me to create a system to auto-backup my changes periodically with a “backer-upper” script so I can easily revert, along with frequent git commits — and PUSHES. About git repos And it is that this point where I will tell you I do NOT give Q access to submit to or access GitHub repositories (soon to become Code Commit repos now that that is back). I have had Q kindly “revert” my changes before I realized what it was doing wiping out a whole day of code. That’s when the backer-upper script came into play. Amazon Q has a way of creating checkpoints of some kind but I haven’t tried it, nor do I trust it if Q has any access to roll back to a particular checkpoint. Smaller projects It was at this point I started moving my code to smaller projects. In theory you should open a Q session in a folder and it should stay in that folder. But it doesn’t. It was easier though to realize when Q was asking to alter a project in another directory. But still not good enough. Common tests in a separate repository To fix issues with Q trying to change the test instead of fixing the offending code I started putting common tests in a separate repository. That caused Q to ask me before changing code in the other project and was easier to spot. But still not good enough. Custom CLI agents I figured out that you could create custom agents in Q. Cool. Each agent has it’s own context and can have global or agent-specific context and rules. There’s a configuration file where you can define which tools are trusted and available to the agent. You can define a local context file and a few other configuration options — but none of that seems to work consistently. It feels like perhaps a “suggestion” rather than a rule. Not good enough. Script to Create an Amazon Q CLI Agent With Custom Context An agent framework Next I tried to create an agent framework to lock down agents using Linux permissions. The problem was I started in my home directory but that was a complete mess. I ended up locking my user out while trying to lock down agents. But I created scripts that I could use to build, test, install, and run rust projects in different folders where I would start project specific agents to modify code in that directory roughly locked down to the correct directories via a Linux user for that project. I ended up moving the projects to a shared directory and set it up so the agents could all execute the shared tests (build, test, install, run) and view all the code in all the projects but not change it. But each agent could modify the code in it’s own directory, install a test version of the project I was working on in a directory specific to that project, write logs specific to that project, and so on. I also wrote scripts that can initialize a new project, start an agent, stop an agent, or stop all agents. Initializing a new project includes: Creating the project directory Creating an agent and project-specific Linux user Creating a GitHub repo (soon to be CodeCommit in a private network with MFA for EACH code commit which you can’t do anywhere else as far as I can tell) Creating a new rust project Creating initial tests and test configuration Configuring the AI agent with an agent-specific context file Pushing a common context file to the agent Checking in the initial code Setting up all the permissions correctly Running test and verify they work I’m probably forgetting something but that’s the gist of it. I have a script to start using an agent. When I run it lists all my projects and I choose the one I want to work on. When I start it up it shows which agent I’m using with Amazon Q CLI. Now when my agent tries to go off and change code in some other project or a project that is designated to run tests the agent can’t touch that code. Once it figures out it doesn’t have permission to change that other code it generally reverts to changing it’s own code without me even telling it to do that. Limited blast radius Now with all of that I can quickly create a new projects configured to run tests the way I want with a new agent and the blast radius for each project and agent is limited to a specific directory and a limited set of code. Cool. Can’t update… Now along comes new versions of Q and Kiro and I can’t update the code. Why? Because it only will update if you are updating the installation in your own home directory. I got a bit stuck at that point and now I’m just considering if I should update or finish what I’m doing first, because I heard Kiro CLI is basically the same, just rebranded. I will update eventually because I’m sure it will improve but I was trying to finish something. Hmm. Backwards compatible but… I looked through the documentation and it should be mostly backwards compatible to what I have and you can even still use the old commands apparently. Essentially I want to rewrite a bunch of scripts to use the Kiro constructs like a steering doc instead of a rules file. (Isn’t rules much clearer? Someone talked to me about a steering doc and I was like a what ?) Wasted time and energy… Now q-start.sh so clean and simple becomes kiro-start.sh and so on if I want to bother to rename everything. Too bad Q got off to a rough start and someone thought rebranding would help. I wish it was still Q to be honest. People will figure out that it got better. I made this same argument when someone wanted to rename another service. Really not necessary. Just fix what you have and call it new and improved. Now it’s just confusing and I have to spend time on nonsense that slows me down from actually writing useful code. But that’s all a tangent. It was actually not that hard to get Kiro installed and “working.” The problem is that it bugs me that all my scripts are still using q commands and have q names but I’ll fix that later. Upgrade Amazon Q CLI to Kiro CLI Not super scalable This agent framework works for me but it’s not super scalable. Anyone using what I have right now could easily change the scripts and files and mess it all up. You have to be security conscious, aware, and use the correct scripts to keep each agent in it’s own little sandbox. You need to trust the developers using it to do the right thing — if they understand what the right thing is and why they are doing it. I have some ideas to get around that problem but I’m just building tools for myself to use on pentests for the moment, not a commercial product, so this is good enough for me. Someone might be able to take these ideas a bit further — and in fact if you are using autonomous agents in applications, Amazon has basically created something like the above with Bedrock Agent Core. Each agent is locked down so it can’t access another agent’s session and so on. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore - AWS Other problems to solve Now solving the security issue was just one of the problems I had to solve on the road to production code. Locking down the agent and limiting what a rogue agent or code injected into a resource it’s reading, the model, or some copy and pasted prompt is one thing. Getting production ready code that works is another. Moving the code to separate project and locking it down was a major leap forward because I can now more easily maintain architectural constructs like traits and factories used to implement common code in a consistent way. However, I’m still having issues getting Q to follow my instructions precisely and not have my context window fill up and then I lose all the detailed context I’ve been working on when it “summarizes” everything and loses important details in the process. Supposedly this was doing to be resolved at re:Invent somehow but I haven’t really seen what solves my specific problems. I already use tests (which basically work like Cedar sidecars in the AI keynote), small focused projects, and specifically formatted requirements in my context. The only thing I saw was a visual to view what Q is going to build before it builds it via a design diagram. That looks somewhat useful but seems like you’d only get that in the IDE version of Kiro. And…I’ve kind of already solved that by breaking my projects down into separate components per project. I ask Q to print out the list of steps it is going to take and check off each one. The problem is when context fills up and I lose my carefully honed list of steps that I finally got the model to abide by. A diagram doesn’t really solve the problem of not following steps in order as far as I can tell. But: I need to upgrade to Kiro and try out autonomous agents and other AWS features announced at re:Invent to see if an how they resolve issues I’ve been having. Likely I’ve missed something or I’m doing something wrong. I have some other ideas that might help which I got from another AWS hero while at re:Invent, so I’m going to check that out and see if it works. Update: I already updated to Kiro and tried my commands again and still have the same problem with steps being executed out of order. I’ll have to try my other ideas to see if I can fix that problem another way. Stay tuned…. In my last post I wrote about how someone who is a complete newbie to AI and not that technical could start writing software…but also demonstrating how having software development expertise can help improve the results.

Hank’s First AI Program

One of the things I mentioned you should be wary of is letting an agent have complete network and file system access to all the things. In this post I’ll give a high level overview of how I’m solving the problem of unrestricted agents.

After about two minutes of using Amazon Q (now Kiro) I was like NOPE. You’re not getting all that access. NO WAY.

Why? Prompt injection, for one thing:

Considering the Likelihood and Impact of AI Chatbot Prompt Injection and Minimizing the Risk

And in general AI agents taking actions I don’t expect or didn’t mean to authorize. Agents are very “creative” at finding ways to fulfill your tasks and solve problems in ways that are not exactly ideal.

A specific Linux user with limited permissions

I started off by trying to figure out how I could use a specific Linux user to run Q which only had permission to work in a specific project directory and could only access certain files and take certain actions.

That’s the solution in a nutshell…but…

Software architecture problems

The next problem I had trying to use Amazon Q was that it was changing code I didn’t want it to change. I would build a complex architecture and it would start rewriting parts of the architecture I didn’t want it touch when I asked or a change. No don’t change that change this.

Test problems

Similar to architecture problems when I tried to run tests and have Q automatically fix the problems, it would change the TEST instead of fixing the CODE with the problem! Creative and all but…not exactly what I had in mind.

Prompt harder doesn’t work

Prompting harder to try to tell Q to do this and not do that (well I think it’s Claude actually but you know what I mean) did not seem to solve the problem. Sometimes Q reads some parts of the prompt but not others.

Context rules don’t work

I tried creating context and rules to get Q to follow them across multiple projects. Nope. Sometimes I could get it to work but reiterating the rules or getting Q to print out the rules and check off each one as it goes. I’m still struggling with these things but regardless if I could get that to work, it was not concrete enough for my security needs.

And when you weren’t looking…

It’s easy to miss something while vibe coding (at least for me) because I want to go fast and I started using multiple agents at once. More on that later. And though I was trying to watch each action I had Q completely delete some of my code multiple times. This led me to create a system to auto-backup my changes periodically with a “backer-upper” script so I can easily revert, along with frequent git commits — and PUSHES.

About git repos

And it is that this point where I will tell you I do NOT give Q access to submit to or access GitHub repositories (soon to become Code Commit repos now that that is back). I have had Q kindly “revert” my changes before I realized what it was doing wiping out a whole day of code. That’s when the backer-upper script came into play. Amazon Q has a way of creating checkpoints of some kind but I haven’t tried it, nor do I trust it if Q has any access to roll back to a particular checkpoint.

Smaller projects

It was at this point I started moving my code to smaller projects. In theory you should open a Q session in a folder and it should stay in that folder. But it doesn’t. It was easier though to realize when Q was asking to alter a project in another directory. But still not good enough.

Common tests in a separate repository

To fix issues with Q trying to change the test instead of fixing the offending code I started putting common tests in a separate repository. That caused Q to ask me before changing code in the other project and was easier to spot. But still not good enough.

Custom CLI agents

I figured out that you could create custom agents in Q. Cool. Each agent has it’s own context and can have global or agent-specific context and rules. There’s a configuration file where you can define which tools are trusted and available to the agent. You can define a local context file and a few other configuration options — but none of that seems to work consistently. It feels like perhaps a “suggestion” rather than a rule. Not good enough.

Script to Create an Amazon Q CLI Agent With Custom Context

An agent framework

Next I tried to create an agent framework to lock down agents using Linux permissions. The problem was I started in my home directory but that was a complete mess. I ended up locking my user out while trying to lock down agents. But I created scripts that I could use to build, test, install, and run rust projects in different folders where I would start project specific agents to modify code in that directory roughly locked down to the correct directories via a Linux user for that project.

I ended up moving the projects to a shared directory and set it up so the agents could all execute the shared tests (build, test, install, run) and view all the code in all the projects but not change it. But each agent could modify the code in it’s own directory, install a test version of the project I was working on in a directory specific to that project, write logs specific to that project, and so on.

I also wrote scripts that can initialize a new project, start an agent, stop an agent, or stop all agents. Initializing a new project includes:

  • Creating the project directory
  • Creating an agent and project-specific Linux user
  • Creating a GitHub repo (soon to be CodeCommit in a private network with MFA for EACH code commit which you can’t do anywhere else as far as I can tell)
  • Creating a new rust project
  • Creating initial tests and test configuration
  • Configuring the AI agent with an agent-specific context file
  • Pushing a common context file to the agent
  • Checking in the initial code
  • Setting up all the permissions correctly
  • Running test and verify they work

I’m probably forgetting something but that’s the gist of it.

I have a script to start using an agent. When I run it lists all my projects and I choose the one I want to work on. When I start it up it shows which agent I’m using with Amazon Q CLI.

Now when my agent tries to go off and change code in some other project or a project that is designated to run tests the agent can’t touch that code. Once it figures out it doesn’t have permission to change that other code it generally reverts to changing it’s own code without me even telling it to do that.

Limited blast radius

Now with all of that I can quickly create a new projects configured to run tests the way I want with a new agent and the blast radius for each project and agent is limited to a specific directory and a limited set of code. Cool.

Can’t update…

Now along comes new versions of Q and Kiro and I can’t update the code. Why? Because it only will update if you are updating the installation in your own home directory. I got a bit stuck at that point and now I’m just considering if I should update or finish what I’m doing first, because I heard Kiro CLI is basically the same, just rebranded. I will update eventually because I’m sure it will improve but I was trying to finish something. Hmm.

Backwards compatible but…

I looked through the documentation and it should be mostly backwards compatible to what I have and you can even still use the old commands apparently. Essentially I want to rewrite a bunch of scripts to use the Kiro constructs like a steering doc instead of a rules file. (Isn’t rules much clearer? Someone talked to me about a steering doc and I was like a what?)

Wasted time and energy…

Now q-start.sh so clean and simple becomes kiro-start.sh and so on if I want to bother to rename everything. Too bad Q got off to a rough start and someone thought rebranding would help. I wish it was still Q to be honest. People will figure out that it got better. I made this same argument when someone wanted to rename another service. Really not necessary. Just fix what you have and call it new and improved. Now it’s just confusing and I have to spend time on nonsense that slows me down from actually writing useful code. But that’s all a tangent.

It was actually not that hard to get Kiro installed and “working.” The problem is that it bugs me that all my scripts are still using q commands and have q names but I’ll fix that later.

Upgrade Amazon Q CLI to Kiro CLI

Not super scalable

This agent framework works for me but it’s not super scalable. Anyone using what I have right now could easily change the scripts and files and mess it all up. You have to be security conscious, aware, and use the correct scripts to keep each agent in it’s own little sandbox. You need to trust the developers using it to do the right thing — if they understand what the right thing is and why they are doing it.

I have some ideas to get around that problem but I’m just building tools for myself to use on pentests for the moment, not a commercial product, so this is good enough for me. Someone might be able to take these ideas a bit further — and in fact if you are using autonomous agents in applications, Amazon has basically created something like the above with Bedrock Agent Core. Each agent is locked down so it can’t access another agent’s session and so on.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore - AWS

Other problems to solve

Now solving the security issue was just one of the problems I had to solve on the road to production code. Locking down the agent and limiting what a rogue agent or code injected into a resource it’s reading, the model, or some copy and pasted prompt is one thing. Getting production ready code that works is another.

Moving the code to separate project and locking it down was a major leap forward because I can now more easily maintain architectural constructs like traits and factories used to implement common code in a consistent way. However, I’m still having issues getting Q to follow my instructions precisely and not have my context window fill up and then I lose all the detailed context I’ve been working on when it “summarizes” everything and loses important details in the process.

Supposedly this was doing to be resolved at re:Invent somehow but I haven’t really seen what solves my specific problems. I already use tests (which basically work like Cedar sidecars in the AI keynote), small focused projects, and specifically formatted requirements in my context.

The only thing I saw was a visual to view what Q is going to build before it builds it via a design diagram. That looks somewhat useful but seems like you’d only get that in the IDE version of Kiro. And…I’ve kind of already solved that by breaking my projects down into separate components per project. I ask Q to print out the list of steps it is going to take and check off each one. The problem is when context fills up and I lose my carefully honed list of steps that I finally got the model to abide by. A diagram doesn’t really solve the problem of not following steps in order as far as I can tell.

But:

  1. I need to upgrade to Kiro and try out autonomous agents and other AWS features announced at re:Invent to see if an how they resolve issues I’ve been having. Likely I’ve missed something or I’m doing something wrong.
  2. I have some other ideas that might help which I got from another AWS hero while at re:Invent, so I’m going to check that out and see if it works.

Update: I already updated to Kiro and tried my commands again and still have the same problem with steps being executed out of order. I’ll have to try my other ideas to see if I can fix that problem another way.

Stay tuned….

items.title: Hank’s First AI Program
items.summary: Explaining generative AI through a simple old-school program written by grade-schoolers on a Commodore 64 back in the 80's ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ⚙️ Security Automation (Pre-AI). The Code . ⚙️ AI Automation . The Code . 🔒 Related Stories: Cybersecurity | Penetration Tests 💻 Free Content on Jobs in Cybersecurity | ✉️ Sign up for the Email List ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ This image was generated by Nano Banana My husband is not a technical person. Even so, back in the day he attended a grade school where he had the opportunity to write a little program on a Commodore 64 many, many years ago. He has told me before about the “turtle that walks in a square.” Meanwhile, I just got back from AWS re:Invent which is Amazon’s largest tech conference where you get to hear all about cutting edge technology used to build and host technology products and services a lot of people use. Companies like Apple, Lyft, and Netflix host their services on AWS. Their developers write and deploy applications on Amazon Web Services using lots of different building blocks faster than if they build everything from scratch using their own systems and code. AI was all the rage at AWS re:Invent again this year. Specifically generative AI and agentic AI. I’ve been using AI to write a lot of code in the last few months to analyze the security of the tools that write the code and the quality of the code they produce. I’ve also been using it to write some of the tools I use on penetration tests where I evaluate the security of customer systems hosted on AWS. To explain what I’ve been doing with AI to him and the kind of things were were talking about at that conference, I opened a tool I’m running on a machine and showed him how he would create that same turtle program today — with generative AI. (More details on how to get set up with the tools below if this interests you.) I logged into my computer, started my AI chatbot used specifically to write code named Amazon Q CLI (now renamed Kiro CLI). First I asked it to write me a turtle program. I simply type: give me a program where a turtle walks in a square in bash Note that I am specific about which programming language to use (bash) but you don’t even have to tell it that if you don’t want to. You’ll just have to know how to execute the resulting code. Bash is simplest. For some reason I repeated the prompt (instructions) and inadvertently asked it to write a turtle walking in a circle: I realized it was trying to write a file to a project directory where I didn’t want the file so I asked it to write to my home directory instead: write it to my home directory I let it create the file, changed the permissions and executed it. Here’s where I noticed my mistake. Not only is the program not writing a square, it’s technically not a circle either. But that wasn’t what we wanted anyway. Back to our square. This is your first AI vibe coding security warning. The fact that I can tell it to write a file anywhere on my machine that I have access and it is not restricted to my project directory could lead to a security problem. I’ve also had it try to use administrator permissions to write or read files and access AWS credentials when it shouldn’t. If you have these tools running on your machine and they can be tricked into accessing sensitive data or writing malware to your machine you might end up having a bad day. What if you have a crypto key (the equivalent of digital money) on your system and you get tricked into sending that money to someone else on the network. What if you get tricked into running commands that connect to other systems on the network that host sensitive data or control access to your network? What if the tools can access your banking credentials stored in your browser password manager? When you start writing code with AI it’s easy to stop paying attention to every detail. It’s writing code so fast that you might not notice it changed a sensitive system file or wrote some questionable action to your startup file (bashrc). It may have written some software that does something you absolutely don’t want. This has happened to me before. I inadvertently authorized an action that deleted a bunch of my code! Explaining generative AI through a simple old-school program written by grade-schoolers on a Commodore 64 back in the 80's

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

⚙️ Security Automation (Pre-AI). The Code.

⚙️ AI Automation. The Code.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This image was generated by Nano Banana

My husband is not a technical person. Even so, back in the day he attended a grade school where he had the opportunity to write a little program on a Commodore 64 many, many years ago. He has told me before about the “turtle that walks in a square.”

Meanwhile, I just got back from AWS re:Invent which is Amazon’s largest tech conference where you get to hear all about cutting edge technology used to build and host technology products and services a lot of people use. Companies like Apple, Lyft, and Netflix host their services on AWS. Their developers write and deploy applications on Amazon Web Services using lots of different building blocks faster than if they build everything from scratch using their own systems and code.

AI was all the rage at AWS re:Invent again this year. Specifically generative AI and agentic AI. I’ve been using AI to write a lot of code in the last few months to analyze the security of the tools that write the code and the quality of the code they produce. I’ve also been using it to write some of the tools I use on penetration tests where I evaluate the security of customer systems hosted on AWS.

To explain what I’ve been doing with AI to him and the kind of things were were talking about at that conference, I opened a tool I’m running on a machine and showed him how he would create that same turtle program today — with generative AI. (More details on how to get set up with the tools below if this interests you.)

I logged into my computer, started my AI chatbot used specifically to write code named Amazon Q CLI (now renamed Kiro CLI).

First I asked it to write me a turtle program.

I simply type:

give me a program where a turtle walks in a square in bash

Note that I am specific about which programming language to use (bash) but you don’t even have to tell it that if you don’t want to. You’ll just have to know how to execute the resulting code. Bash is simplest.

For some reason I repeated the prompt (instructions) and inadvertently asked it to write a turtle walking in a circle:

I realized it was trying to write a file to a project directory where I didn’t want the file so I asked it to write to my home directory instead:

write it to my home directory

I let it create the file, changed the permissions and executed it.

Here’s where I noticed my mistake. Not only is the program not writing a square, it’s technically not a circle either. But that wasn’t what we wanted anyway. Back to our square.

This is your first AI vibe coding security warning. The fact that I can tell it to write a file anywhere on my machine that I have access and it is not restricted to my project directory could lead to a security problem.

I’ve also had it try to use administrator permissions to write or read files and access AWS credentials when it shouldn’t. If you have these tools running on your machine and they can be tricked into accessing sensitive data or writing malware to your machine you might end up having a bad day.

What if you have a crypto key (the equivalent of digital money) on your system and you get tricked into sending that money to someone else on the network. What if you get tricked into running commands that connect to other systems on the network that host sensitive data or control access to your network? What if the tools can access your banking credentials stored in your browser password manager?

When you start writing code with AI it’s easy to stop paying attention to every detail. It’s writing code so fast that you might not notice it changed a sensitive system file or wrote some questionable action to your startup file (bashrc). It may have written some software that does something you absolutely don’t want.

This has happened to me before. I inadvertently authorized an action that deleted a bunch of my code! Luckily I make lots of backups while I’m using these tools. I’ve also written a framework to lock them down … more on that here:

Agents in Sandboxes

That’s why initially you should carefully review each action and type y (yes) not t (trust) when it comes to executable actions and writing files.

So here’s where I attempt to fix the program:

that was a circle, not a square

The results were not promising:

I attempt to correct the problem by getting Q (now Kiro) to tell me what a square is in an attempt to get it “thinking” about the right solution:

It recognizes that is not a square and tries to fix the program:

Hmm. Not exactly…

Let’s ask it a question to see if it thinks it has succeeded. This is one of my tricks for getting the AI tools to produce what I want. Sometimes it works.

Still not working…I give more information to try to get it to solve the problem. This is an example of how and why you need to get your prompts (instructions) right to get the results you want. Ambiguous prompts may get you started but then you have to be more specific:

A square has four equal sides and your sides are not equal. You have to take into account spaces and gaps on the screen when you print out the characters

YAY. A square. But Hank is not satisfied. The program he wrote had solid lines. I’ll let you just look through these to see the results. I did not include every screen shot below but you can see the problems and how I tried to fix them:

After many more iterations…

Finally!

Here’s the full program:

That code is a bit complicated. Let’s see if we can simplify it.

That code does almost the same thing but it’s much simpler. And that example shows why more lines of code doesn’t mean the program is better or doing more or programmers that write more code are more productive.

In fact, how the dashboard in the post below calculate line lines of code from that last request? Did it add to the lines of code I accepted? Did it reduce the number of lines of code accepted?

Lines of Code Accepted is an Absolutely Meaningless Metric

There is one small problem with the rewrite however. There’s an extra character in the output. And this shows you why having programmer guiding the process is going to produce better results than having just anyone trying to write code with tools like this.

I ask Q (now Kiro) to fix the problem.

After multiple rounds the AI agent is struggling, so I went and actually reviewed the code. I found the offending character in the code.

I modified the code to exit before that line, and no special character.

Then after that line — the extraneous character shows up.

I commented out the special character and the top right corner of the box AND the floating character is gone.

With that bit of troubleshooting, now I can tell the AI tool exactly where the problem is so it focuses it’s efforts on fixing that one line:

And with a little bit of programming knowledge in the mix the AI tools stop going in circles (sometimes) and you can get the result you want.

But not just yet. My husband said the turtle was going too fast.

I ask to slow the turtle down…

And that’s where the whole program got messed up again. It slowed down the top and right but when it tried to slow down the bottom line it disappeared again. This is what happens when you’re vibe coding. A lot of times you can get the first cut right but when you attempt to modify the program things go haywire.

Well this is just a silly little program to demonstrate a few concepts so I’m not going to spend more time on it, but that gives you an idea what it’s like to “vibe code.”

How to get started

A lot of developers are actually using visual coding environments called IDEs (integrated development environments) like Kiro IDE which you can download and install as explained here:

Installation - IDE - Docs - Kiro

I like using a terminal window as shown above for the reasons explained here:

CLI vs. IDE for AI Coding 💪

I have an AI tool called Amazon Q CLI installed which has been rebranded to Kiro CLI. It works the same way but it has some different commands.

Kiro: Agentic AI development from prototype to production

You can download and install the visual version of Kiro and run it on your laptop or run it on a remote computer as I do using a terminal window. This page explains how to install Kiro CLI:

Installation - CLI - Docs - Kiro

Once you install the program, you will need to login.

Authentication methods - CLI - Docs - Kiro

Once you are logged in…start asking questions. That’s it!

Install the program, login, start asking questions.

Now consider where you are installing the program. I install the program on a computer running in the cloud in a locked down network, not on my laptop. That helps me reduce the risk of the AI tools getting access to sensitive data on my laptop or home network.

When I wanted to show my husband the simple programming steps above, I logged into AWS and started a computer (called an EC2 instance) I have running on AWS. I connected to the remote computer using SSH. I logged in, ran the tool, and asked the questions above on my computer running in the cloud.

You’ll still want to learn to program to be a good vibe coder, but you can learn so much faster. I learned to program in rust — something I have been putting off for a long time but wanted to do — in about a day:

Getting Amazon Q to Help Write Production Ready Rust Code

Artificial Intelligence
